quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten checks on container loading, export charges, sale proceeds and contribution per metre and per loom.

questions.q: What limits the quantity of grey fabric loaded into the 40 ft container in this lecture?
questions.explain: Grey fabric is dense, so the weight limit binds before the volume: 57,000 lb ÷ 0.529 lb per metre ≈ 107,745 m.

questions.q: Which of these export charges is quoted per container in rupees rather than in dollars?
questions.explain: Transport to port (Rs 15,000), forwarding and local bank charges are rupee costs; ocean freight and foreign bank charges are in US dollars and converted at the exchange rate.

questions.q: The export surcharge and the commission are both percentages of the sale proceeds.
questions.explain: Surcharge 0.25 % and commission 1 % of Rs 42 give Rs 0.105 and Rs 0.42 per metre; they rise and fall with the price, unlike the per-container charges.

questions.q: Sale proceeds per metre in rupees are…
options: US$ price per metre × exchange rate
US$ price per metre ÷ exchange rate
US$ price per metre × metres per container
questions.explain: US$ 0.70 × Rs 60 = Rs 42.00 per metre. Dividing would give a fraction of a rupee.

questions.q: Contribution margin per metre is…
options: sale proceeds − variable production cost − export cost
questions.explain: Rs 42.00 − Rs 30.32 (production plus export variable cost) = Rs 11.68. Leaving out either part overstates the margin.

questions.q: Why is contribution expressed per loom per day?
options: Because looms are sold with the fabric
To compare it with the loom's daily fixed cost and decide whether the order is worth taking
Because freight is charged per loom
questions.explain: The loom is the scarce resource: Rs 11.68 × 434.5 m = Rs 5,073 a day against a fixed cost of about Rs 4,000 (Lecture 8) shows the order is worth taking, but only just.

questions.q: The yarn weight used to load the container includes contraction but not wastage or B-grade. Why?
options: Only the yarn actually in the cloth travels in the container; waste and rejected cloth do not
It is a simplification with no reason
questions.explain: Loading needs the real weight of the fabric: 0.225 lb of ends × 1.10 crimp = 0.2475 lb of warp per yard, with no allowance for yarn lost before weaving.

questions.q: A 40 ft container carries about 57,000 lb, which is roughly 25.9 tonnes.
questions.explain: 57,000 ÷ 2.2046 ≈ 25,855 kg. That is the payload figure the lecture uses for grey fabric.

questions.q: Forwarding charges are…
options: the freight paid to the shipping line
fees of the clearing and forwarding agent who handles documents and the port, charged per container
the bank's charge for negotiating documents
questions.explain: The forwarder's fee (Rs 3,500 per container here) is distinct from ocean freight (the shipping line) and from bank charges.

questions.q: The lecture says the order is "worth taking — but only just". What makes it marginal?
options: Contribution per loom per day (Rs 5,073) is only about Rs 1,000 above the loom's fixed cost, and a small price change erodes it
questions.explain: With a fixed cost of about Rs 4,000 per loom per day the margin of safety is thin: a one-cent fall in the dollar price takes about Rs 0.59 off each of 434.5 metres, about Rs 256 a day.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: How container quantity, per-metre export charges, proceeds and contribution are computed, and which way each moves.

questions.q: Metres per container equals…
questions.explain: 57,000 ÷ 0.5290 = 107,745 m. Using weight per yard gives yards, and mixing kg with lb gives nonsense.

questions.q: A per-container charge in dollars becomes a cost per metre by…
questions.explain: Ocean freight US$ 500 × 60 = Rs 30,000; ÷ 107,745 m = Rs 0.278 per metre.

questions.q: If the fabric is made heavier (more picks), what happens to the per-container export charges per metre?
options: They rise, because fewer metres fit in the container
questions.explain: A heavier metre means fewer metres per 57,000 lb, so each metre carries a larger share of the fixed charges per box.

questions.q: Total export cost per metre = transport + ocean freight + forwarding + foreign bank + local bank + surcharge + commission.
Contribution per loom per day equals…
options: contribution per metre × loom production per day (m)
contribution per metre ÷ loom production per day
sale proceeds × loom production per day
contribution per metre × metres per container
questions.explain: Rs 11.68 × 434.5 m = Rs 5,073. Using proceeds instead of contribution ignores the Rs 30.32 of variable cost.

questions.q: If the exchange rate rises from Rs 60 to Rs 66 (price fixed at US$ 0.70), what happens to proceeds per metre and to contribution?
options: Proceeds rise to Rs 46.20 and contribution rises by nearly Rs 4.20 per metre
questions.explain: Proceeds = 0.70 × 66 = Rs 46.20, up Rs 4.20. Dollar costs (freight and foreign bank, Rs 0.39 per metre) rise by Rs 0.04 and surcharge plus commission by Rs 0.05, so contribution rises by about Rs 4.11.

questions.q: A one-cent fall in the dollar price per metre at Rs 60 per dollar reduces proceeds by…
questions.explain: US$ 0.01 × Rs 60 = Rs 0.60 per metre; after the 1.25 % of commission and surcharge saved it is about Rs 0.59 off contribution, roughly a twentieth of the margin.

questions.q: Which of the export costs per metre does NOT depend on the number of metres per container?
questions.explain: Commission is 1 % of proceeds per metre regardless of loading; the per-container charges are all divided by metres per container.

questions.q: Yarn weight per metre is found from the weight per yard by multiplying by 1.0936.
questions.explain: 0.4838 lb per yard × 1.0936 = 0.5290 lb per metre; a metre is longer than a yard so it holds more yarn.

questions.q: If loom efficiency rises so the loom makes 458 m a day instead of 434.5 m, contribution per loom per day…
options: rises in proportion to about Rs 5,350
questions.explain: Rs 11.68 × 458 ≈ Rs 5,350. Contribution per metre is unchanged; more metres a day simply earn more against the same fixed cost.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Compute container quantity, export charges per metre, proceeds, contribution per metre and contribution per loom per day.

questions.q: Warp yarn in one yard of fabric is 0.2250 lb before crimp and warp contraction is 10 %. What is the warp weight per yard with contraction (four decimals)?
questions.explain: 0.2250 × 1.10 = 0.2475 lb per yard, the sheet's row 7.

questions.q: Warp 0.2475 lb and weft 0.2363 lb per yard. Convert the total to lb per metre (1 m = 1.0936 yd), to four decimals.
questions.explain: 0.4838 lb per yard × 1.0936 = 0.5291 lb per metre (0.5290 in the sheet).

questions.q: A 40 ft container carries 57,000 lb and the fabric weighs 0.5290 lb per metre. How many metres fit, to the nearest metre?
questions.explain: 57,000 ÷ 0.5290 = 107,750 m (the sheet shows 107,745 with unrounded weight).

questions.q: Ocean freight is US$ 500 per container at Rs 60 per dollar and the container holds 107,745 m. What is the ocean freight per metre, to three decimals?
Transport to port costs Rs 15,000 per container of 107,745 m. What is the cost per metre, to three decimals?
The fabric sells at US$ 0.70 per metre at Rs 60 per dollar. Commission is 1 % and the export surcharge 0.25 % of proceeds. What is the combined commission and surcharge per metre, to three decimals?
questions.explain: Proceeds = Rs 42.00; 1.25 % of 42 = Rs 0.525 per metre (0.42 + 0.105).

questions.q: Sale proceeds are Rs 42.00 per metre and total variable cost (production plus export) is Rs 30.32. What is the contribution per metre?
questions.explain: Rs 42.00 − Rs 30.32 = Rs 11.68 per metre.

questions.q: Contribution is Rs 11.68 per metre and a loom makes 434.5 m a day. What is the contribution per loom per day, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 11.68 × 434.5 = Rs 5,075 (Rs 5,073 in the sheet with the unrounded 11.675).

questions.q: Total export cost per metre is Rs 1.114 and the variable production cost is Rs 29.21. What is the total variable cost per metre?
questions.explain: 29.21 + 1.114 = Rs 30.32. Rs 28.10 subtracts the export cost instead of adding it.

questions.q: Contribution per loom per day is Rs 5,073 and the loom's fixed cost is Rs 4,000 a day. What is the profit per loom per day?
questions.explain: Rs 5,073 − Rs 4,000 = Rs 1,073 per loom per day, a thin margin on a Rs 42 product.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Decisions in an export costing office: negotiating cents, choosing payment terms, and reacting to freight and exchange-rate changes.

questions.q: The buyer asks for a price cut from US$ 0.70 to US$ 0.68 per metre. With contribution per loom per day at Rs 5,073 and fixed cost about Rs 4,000, should the mill agree?
options: Two cents is about Rs 1.19 per metre after commission and surcharge, about Rs 515 per loom per day; the order still covers fixed cost but with a very thin margin
No, the order would lose money immediately
questions.explain: 2 × Rs 0.59 ≈ Rs 1.19 per metre × 434.5 m ≈ Rs 515 a day, leaving about Rs 4,560 against Rs 4,000 fixed cost. Acceptable only if nothing else goes wrong.

questions.q: Ocean freight doubles from US$ 500 to US$ 1,000 per container. Effect on contribution per metre?
options: No effect because the buyer pays
questions.explain: Freight per metre goes from Rs 0.278 to Rs 0.556, a fall of Rs 0.278 in contribution; small per metre, about Rs 120 per loom per day.

questions.q: Because export charges per metre are only about Rs 1.11, a costing office may safely ignore them when quoting.
questions.explain: Rs 1.11 is nearly a tenth of the Rs 11.68 contribution; ignoring it overstates contribution per loom per day by about Rs 480 and could turn a marginal order into a loss.

questions.q: A merchant offers to take the goods FOB (buyer pays ocean freight) at US$ 0.695 instead of US$ 0.70 with freight paid by the mill. Which is better per metre?
options: US$ 0.70 with freight, by about Rs 0.02
questions.explain: Half a cent is Rs 0.30 of proceeds (about Rs 0.296 after commission and surcharge); freight saved is Rs 0.278. The mill keeps about Rs 0.02 more per metre at US$ 0.70, so there is little in it.

questions.q: The dyeing department wants the same looms for a dyed-fabric order earning Rs 5,500 contribution per loom per day. What should the costing office recommend?
options: Keep the grey order; it is already profitable
Give the looms to the order with the higher contribution per loom per day, the dyed order, if its figures are sound
Choose the order with the higher price per metre
questions.explain: When looms are the scarce resource, contribution per loom per day is the right basis for ranking orders, exactly as frames were ranked in Lecture 17.

questions.q: A clerk uses the yarn weight including wastage and B-grade (0.5082 lb per yard) to load the container. What is the effect?
options: Metres per container is understated, so export charges per metre are overstated
questions.explain: A heavier assumed metre means fewer metres per 57,000 lb; the real fabric weighs only 0.4838 lb per yard, so the real container holds more and charges per metre are lower.

questions.q: The rupee strengthens from Rs 60 to Rs 57 per dollar during the order. What happens to the mill?
options: Proceeds fall by Rs 2.10 per metre and the order is close to loss-making
No change because the contract is in dollars
questions.explain: 0.70 × 57 = Rs 39.90, down Rs 2.10; contribution falls to about Rs 9.6 per metre and about Rs 4,180 per loom per day, barely above Rs 4,000 fixed cost. Export mills watch the rupee daily.

questions.q: Reducing B-grade would raise contribution per loom per day both by increasing A-grade metres and by lowering yarn cost per metre.
questions.explain: More metres a day at Rs 11.68 each, and a lower ÷ (1 − B) grossing of yarn in Lecture 18. Quality improvement pays twice.

questions.q: The forwarder proposes loading 20 ft containers (payload about 28,000 lb) at Rs 10,000 transport each instead of 40 ft at Rs 15,000. Which is cheaper per metre for transport to port?
questions.explain: 20 ft: 28,000 ÷ 0.529 ≈ 52,930 m, Rs 10,000 ÷ 52,930 = Rs 0.189 per metre; 40 ft: Rs 0.139. The 40 ft box is about Rs 0.05 per metre cheaper.

questions.q: Management asks for the price at which the order exactly covers the Rs 4,000 loom fixed cost. Which approach is correct?
options: Find the contribution per metre needed (4,000 ÷ 434.5 ≈ Rs 9.21), add variable cost and adjust for commission and surcharge, then convert to dollars
Divide Rs 4,000 by the exchange rate
Set price equal to variable cost per metre
Use US$ 0.70 since that is the market
questions.explain: Required contribution Rs 9.21 + Rs 29.81 (variable cost excluding the 1.25 % items) = Rs 39.02; ÷ 0.9875 = Rs 39.51; ÷ 60 ≈ US$ 0.659 per metre. This is the break-even price.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Two-step reasoning across the whole fabric costing: break-even prices, sensitivity to a cent or a rupee, and common slips with units and loading.

questions.q: Loom fixed cost is Rs 4,000 a day and the loom makes 434.5 m. Variable cost excluding commission and surcharge is Rs 29.81 per metre; commission and surcharge together are 1.25 % of proceeds. Find the break-even price in Rs per metre, to the nearest paisa.
questions.explain: Required contribution = 4,000 ÷ 434.5 = Rs 9.21; price P satisfies 0.9875P = 9.21 + 29.81 = 39.02, so P = Rs 39.51 (US$ 0.659 at Rs 60).

questions.q: A one-cent fall in the dollar price costs Rs 0.59 of contribution per metre. On a loom making 434.5 m a day, how much contribution per loom per day is lost, to the nearest rupee?
questions.explain: 0.59 × 434.5 ≈ Rs 256 a day per loom, about a quarter of the Rs 1,073 profit margin.

questions.q: A costing shows 107,745 m per container but the fabric is quoted per yard. A student divides 57,000 lb by the weight per yard (0.4838 lb) and reports 117,817 m. What is wrong?
options: The result is in yards, not metres; 117,817 yd = 107,745 m
The payload should be in kg
The weight per yard should include wastage
questions.explain: Dividing pounds by pounds per yard gives yards. 117,817 yd × 0.9144 = 107,745 m. Unit slips of 9 % are the commonest error in these sheets.

questions.q: A heavier fabric weighs 0.72 lb per metre. How many metres fit in a 57,000 lb container, to the nearest metre?
questions.explain: 57,000 ÷ 0.72 = 79,167 m, so per-container charges per metre rise by 107,745 ÷ 79,167 ≈ 36 %.

questions.q: For the 0.72 lb per metre fabric above, what is the ocean freight per metre at US$ 500 and Rs 60?
questions.explain: Rs 30,000 ÷ 79,167 = Rs 0.379 per metre, against Rs 0.278 for the lighter fabric. Heavy fabrics carry more freight per metre, though usually also a higher price.

questions.q: If the sale price and all costs are unchanged but the loom produces more metres per day, the contribution per metre rises.
questions.explain: Contribution per metre stays Rs 11.68; what rises is contribution per loom per day. Only fixed cost per metre falls with more output.

questions.q: The container's export charges per container total Rs 63,500 (transport Rs 15,000, freight Rs 30,000, forwarding Rs 3,500, foreign bank Rs 12,000, local bank Rs 3,000). Over 107,745 m, what is the per-container charge per metre, to three decimals?
questions.explain: Rs 63,500 ÷ 107,745 = Rs 0.589 per metre; adding commission and surcharge of Rs 0.525 gives the Rs 1.114 total export cost.

questions.q: Two orders: A at US$ 0.70 on a 60-pick fabric (434.5 m a day, contribution Rs 11.68 per metre) and B at US$ 0.80 on an 80-pick fabric of the same yarn (326 m a day, contribution Rs 14.50 per metre). Which earns more per loom per day?
options: A, about Rs 5,073 versus about Rs 4,727
B, because its contribution per metre is higher
questions.explain: A: 11.68 × 434.5 = Rs 5,073. B: 14.50 × 326 = Rs 4,727. The denser fabric earns more per metre but ties up the loom longer, so A wins per loom per day.

questions.q: Proceeds are Rs 42.00 and total variable cost Rs 30.32 per metre. A buyer wants the price reduced so that the mill's contribution per metre is exactly Rs 10.00. Ignoring the 1.25 % commission and surcharge adjustment, what price per metre in rupees is that?
questions.explain: Rs 30.32 + Rs 10.00 = Rs 40.32 per metre (US$ 0.672 at Rs 60). Allowing for the 1.25 % saved on the lower price the exact figure is a few paisa lower.

questions.q: Which statement best summarises the lesson of Lecture 20?
options: Export charges are the largest cost of grey fabric
A grey fabric order is judged by contribution per loom per day against loom fixed cost, and a single cent of price moves that judgement
Containers should always be loaded by volume
questions.explain: Yarn is the largest cost, export charges about Rs 1.11 per metre, and the Rs 5,073 against Rs 4,000 comparison is where the decision is made; a cent is worth Rs 0.59 of an Rs 11.68 margin.
